messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Your previous vignette failed validation. Make ONLY the targeted changes listed below.

Previous vignette:
Arjun, a 29-year-old painter from a South Asian background, found himself ensnared in a web of anxiety and fear following a traumatic mugging last year. The incident had left an indelible mark on him. He vividly recalled the evening when he was walking home from a late job, paintbrushes still tucked under his arm, when a group of men confronted him. He remembered the rush of adrenaline, the fear coursing through his veins as they demanded his wallet and phone. The ordeal lasted mere minutes, but it felt like an eternity, and he would wake up in a cold sweat, haunted by nightmares of the event—dreams where he relived the moment again and again, the panic rising in his chest as he struggled to break free. Each time he awoke, he felt a surge of irritability, an angry outburst bubbling just beneath the surface. It was as if he had become a stranger to himself, his body always on high alert, constantly scanning his surroundings for potential threats. 

The physical locations where the mugging had occurred became charged with anxiety. Simply passing by those streets triggered a rush of intrusive memories, causing his heart to race and his palms to sweat. These moments magnified the tense state his body had adopted; he felt as if he were perpetually ready to react to danger, a sensation that transformed his daily life into a battleground. The world outside was a constant reminder of his trauma, and each spatial trigger intensified his belief that he could no longer trust the people around him. He had come to mistrust everyone, convinced that anyone could become a threat, and this growing isolation made him feel more detached from those he loved. 

As he grappled with these feelings, Arjun found it difficult to piece together the memory of the mugging. He often felt as though he was only recalling fragments of the experience, the gaps gnawing at him and fueling his guilt. He would sit in his studio, attempting to deliberate on the event, but the harder he tried to access the painful recollections, the more elusive they became. This incomplete picture of the traumatic event compounded his feelings of guilt; he often questioned why he hadn’t fought back or run faster, which only deepened his sense of inadequacy. The memories, though fragmented, remained potent triggers—each recall would send him spiraling back into that moment of vulnerability, enhancing his sense of danger and leading him to believe that he was incapable of relying on anyone, not even himself.

Arjun's negative appraisals shaped his perception of the world, creating a vicious cycle. His mistrust of people steered him towards isolation, which only fortified his belief that he couldn’t rely on others. As he withdrew from social interactions, he would find himself alone in his thoughts, the memories of the mugging replaying in his mind, reinforcing his feelings of vulnerability. This constant reflection contributed to his irritability and made him more sensitive to perceived slights from others, aggravating his readiness to react defensively. Each day became a struggle as he navigated through the layers of his trauma, caught in an ever-tightening loop of anxiety and avoidance.

When Arjun finally sought help, he felt a glimmer of hope mixed with the fear of confronting his trauma. He harbored a deep-seated worry that delving into his memories would only serve to amplify his feelings of guilt and mistrust, but he knew he could not continue living in this state of hypervigilance. He longed to reclaim the joy he once found in painting, to reconnect with his wife and friends without the shadow of his trauma looming overhead. With each session, he hoped to find a way to unravel the knots of his experience, to understand the connection between the past and present, and to ultimately heal from the scars that had come to define his daily existence.

Issues to fix:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Triggers → Threat: The vignette does not establish a causal relationship where triggers lead to a sense of threat.
  e.g. "The cues led to a feeling of danger that felt as real as the original event."
  e.g. "A knock at the door after dark sent her heart into her throat — her body read it as an emergency, even when her mind knew better."
  e.g. "Sitting in the waiting room, she noticed a man watching her from across the room and felt the same cold certainty: something terrible was about to happen."
- Triggers → Memory: The vignette does not establish a causal relationship where triggers lead to memory.
  e.g. "The smell of his cologne in the lift sent the whole night flooding back before she had even reached her floor."
  e.g. "Hearing that song on the radio dragged her straight back into the room where it happened, as if no time had passed at all."
  e.g. "Walking past the bus stop where it occurred, she was no longer on the street — she was back there, every detail sharp and close."
- Negative Appraisals → Threat: The vignette does not establish a causal relationship where negative appraisals lead to a sense of threat.
  e.g. "Having decided that she was permanently vulnerable, she walked into rooms already braced — the threat arrived with her before anything had happened."
  e.g. "The belief that she was a target — not unlucky, but chosen — meant that every unfamiliar face carried a weight of potential danger."
  e.g. "Her certainty that she couldn't protect herself made every new situation feel like a test she was already failing."
- Negative Appraisals → Triggers: The vignette does not establish a causal relationship where negative appraisals lead to triggers.
  e.g. "Once she had concluded that the world was fundamentally unsafe, almost anything could confirm it — a figure in her periphery, the wrong tone of voice, footsteps behind her."
  e.g. "The belief that she couldn't trust her own judgement meant that things she would once have registered and dismissed now snagged and held her attention."
  e.g. "Her conviction that it would happen again meant she moved through ordinary days as if they were mined — every ambiguity became a potential signal."
- Memory → Threat: The vignette does not establish a causal relationship where memory leads to a sense of threat.
  e.g. "Once the memory had surfaced, she couldn't shake the sense that the danger was still present — that it had simply moved into her body rather than gone away."
  e.g. "The flashback left her standing in her own kitchen feeling hunted, even with the door locked and the lights on."
  e.g. "After the memory broke through, the threat felt immediate and physical — not something that had happened, but something that was still happening."
- Memory → Negative Appraisals: The vignette does not establish a causal relationship where memory leads to negative appraisals.
  e.g. "After the image broke through again, she caught herself thinking: if this keeps happening, there must be something deeply wrong with me."
  e.g. "The memory surfaced in the middle of a meeting and she spent the rest of the day convinced that everyone around her could see how broken she was."
  e.g. "Each time the flashback came, the thought that followed it was always the same — that she had let this happen, and that it said something permanent about who she was."
- Memory → Triggers: The vignette does not establish a causal relationship where memory leads to triggers.
  e.g. "After the memory had surfaced, even the most ordinary things — a kettle whistling, a door slamming — felt like warnings she couldn't afford to ignore."
  e.g. "The intrusive image left her scanning every room she entered, cataloguing exits, tracking faces, unable to switch off."
  e.g. "Because the memory came back so vividly, she began to see threads of it everywhere: in strangers' faces, in certain times of day, in the quality of winter light."
- Threat → Triggers: The vignette does not establish a causal relationship where threat leads to triggers.
  e.g. "Already running on threat, she found that almost anything could tip into a warning — a van parked at an odd angle, a light left on that shouldn't have been."
  e.g. "The background hum of danger she carried everywhere made ordinary cues feel like messages — each one confirming what her body already believed."
  e.g. "Living at that pitch of alertness, she found the world had become dense with reminders she couldn't stop reading."

---

Return ONLY patch blocks — do NOT return the full vignette.

For each REQUIRED EDGE MISSING — produce one INSERT_AFTER block.
Find a paragraph in the vignette that already mentions component A, and add a sentence
after it that shows A influencing B through natural clinical language.
<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
[copy 1–2 sentences from the vignette — the anchor after which to insert]
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
[one or two sentences that convey A influencing B, written as natural clinical prose]
<<<END>>>

Output ONLY these patch blocks. No prose, no explanation, no full vignette.

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
He vividly recalled the evening when he was walking home from a late job, paintbrushes still tucked under his arm, when a group of men confronted him. 
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
The memory of that confrontation loomed heavily in his mind, making every shadow and every unfamiliar figure on the street feel like an imminent threat, as if danger could strike again at any moment. 
<<<END>>>

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
Simply passing by those streets triggered a rush of intrusive memories, causing his heart to race and his palms to sweat. 
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
These memories flooded back with such intensity that they felt alive, forcing him to relive the fear and vulnerability of the event as if it were happening anew, amplifying his sense of threat. 
<<<END>>>

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
He had come to mistrust everyone, convinced that anyone could become a threat, and this growing isolation made him feel more detached from those he loved. 
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
His negative beliefs about his own safety shaped how he viewed the world, instilling a persistent sense of danger that made him hyper-aware of any situation where he might feel exposed or vulnerable. 
<<<END>>>

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
He often felt as though he was only recalling fragments of the experience, the gaps gnawing at him and fueling his guilt. 
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
Each time those fragments surfaced, they deepened his conviction that he had failed to protect himself, reinforcing his belief that he was inadequate and leaving him feeling hopeless and trapped. 
<<<END>>>

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
This constant reflection contributed to his irritability and made him more sensitive to perceived slights from others, aggravating his readiness to react defensively. 
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
His memories of the traumatic event seemed to taunt him, leading him to interpret innocent interactions as threats, convinced that others were judging him or harboring malicious intent. 
<<<END>>>

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
When Arjun finally sought help, he felt a glimmer of hope mixed with the fear of confronting his trauma. 
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
He was acutely aware that the memories he carried would not only resurface but could also amplify his fears, making every session feel like stepping into a minefield of emotions he had long tried to avoid. 
<<<END>>>

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
He longed to reclaim the joy he once found in painting, to reconnect with his wife and friends without the shadow of his trauma looming overhead. 
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
Yet, he feared that engaging with those memories would only serve to reinforce his belief that he was permanently broken, trapped in a cycle of pain and mistrust that he couldn't escape. 
<<<END>>>
